prediction:
THOUGHT: The patient is a young woman with an incidental systolic murmur, dilated right atrium and right ventricle, and a large 21-mm intracardiac defect with a left-to-right shunt on transthoracic echo. Right-sided cath shows a clear step-up in oxygen saturation from the caval veins to the right atrium (SVC 71% and IVC 77% → RA 84%), localizing the shunt at the atrial level. Pulmonary vascular resistance is low (1.8 WU), consistent with a significant but not irreversible left-to-right ASD physiology. The ECG shows complete right bundle-branch block and fragmented QRS in inferior leads, a pattern commonly seen with chronic RV volume overload from an ASD. Taken together, these findings most strongly indicate an atrial septal defect—most likely an ostium secundum ASD. Sinus venosus ASD (often with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return) is the next most likely alternative because it can be missed on TTE and produces similar hemodynamics and an SVC-region step-up. Ostium primum ASD is less likely because there is no PR prolongation or AV-valve abnormality described. A large PFO is unlikely given the size (21 mm) and RA/RV dilation, and ventricular-level shunts would produce a different cath/echo pattern.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Ostium secundum atrial septal defect (secundum ASD / ostium secundum) — most likely
2. Sinus venosus atrial septal defect (often associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous return)
3. Partial anomalous pulmonary venous return (PAPVR) producing an atrial-level shunt (may coexist with sinus venosus ASD)
4. Ostium primum atrial septal defect (atrioventricular septal defect) — less likely
5. Patent foramen ovale (PFO) — unlikely given defect size and chamber enlargement
